title: How Effective Altruism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain effective altruism (EA), a philosophy-rooted movement that emphasizes using evidence and measurable outcomes (such as quality-adjusted life years) to direct charitable giving to the interventions that save or improve the most lives, with impartial weight given to every life regardless of location, and including animals. They cover the movement's origins around 2010, the Center for Effective Altruism, Giving What We Can, 80,000 Hours, GiveWell, Open Philanthropy, pledges, earning to give, the four core commitments per Will MacAskill, utilitarianism and Peter Singer's drowning-child thought experiment, criticisms (overhead of measurement, unquantifiable value, emotional giving, extremism), longtermism and existential risk, and the animal welfare focus on factory farming. The episode opens with a plug for Dick Town and closes with a listener mail from Brett about albinism.

entities.name: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening banter and Dick Town plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck plug the animated show Dick Town (Hodgman and Reese) and introduce the episode topic of effective altruism, noting its link to the earlier short stuff on charitable giving.

segments.title: What effective altruism is and its polarizing reputation
segments.summary: EA is a relatively new movement, roughly from 2010, rooted in utilitarianism. Hosts say criticism often focuses on extremes, and the middle-ground practice is more sensible. They describe the basic idea of calculating giving to save the most lives and the wealth comparison showing even modest donors in the US are rich globally.

segments.title: History and key organizations
segments.summary: Origins of the Center for Effective Altruism umbrella, Giving What We Can founded by Toby Ord and Will MacAskill, and 80,000 Hours founded by MacAskill and Benjamin Todd. Other groups mentioned include The Life You Can Save and Animal Charity Evaluators.

segments.title: Core commitments and impartiality
segments.summary: Will MacAskill's 2018 paper lays out four core commitments: maximizing the good, aligning with science and evidence, welfare, and impartiality. Impartiality means every person's life counts equally, implying donations abroad can do more than local ones, which draws critics' objections about local charities.

segments.title: GiveWell, open philanthropy, and Peter Singer
segments.summary: GiveWell (founded 2007) and Open Philanthropy, backed by Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, are introduced. Utilitarian roots (Bentham, Mill) are noted. Peter Singer's drowning child and new shoes thought experiment from Famine, Affluence and Morality is explained, along with his extreme positions, which the hosts say are not central to EA.

segments.title: Giving statistics, pledges, and earning to give
segments.summary: US charitable giving figures are discussed, with individuals giving most. EA-endorsed pledges include Giving What We Can (10 percent), Founders Pledge, and TryGiving. The 80,000 Hours idea of career choice is explained, including earning to give and choosing impactful work, with examples of an engineer and an Australian epidemiologist.

segments.title: Evidence, randomized controlled trials, and criticisms
segments.summary: EA favors measurable outcomes over overhead ratios, using randomized controlled trials such as a malaria net study. Criticisms include that some value cannot be quantified, using the example of the 1963 March on Washington, and that trial results may not reproduce across time and place. Emotional giving and the cost of trials are also discussed.

segments.title: Animal welfare and factory farming
segments.summary: EA directs attention to factory-farmed animals, which receive about one percent of US charitable spending, compared with donations to companion animal causes. The hosts discuss the utilitarian case based on sheer numbers and note the tension with human causes.

segments.title: Defending EA against extremist associations
segments.summary: Hosts read a Will MacAskill statement that EA does not claim all helping is permissible, has norms against harm, and does not require sacrificing one's own interests. They conclude common sense applies and that giving can be both local and effective.

segments.title: Longtermism and existential risk
segments.summary: Longtermism is explained as prioritizing the vast number of future humans, leading some EA thinkers to focus on existential risks such as climate change and AI. Hosts mention the End of the World podcast and money committed to EA, around 46 billion dollars per Benjamin Todd.

segments.title: Personal reflections on giving
segments.summary: Chuck discusses family giving and supporting Compassion International-style child sponsorship (referred to as CoED in the transcript), arguing that local and effective giving can coexist. Josh summarizes EA as anti-sentimentalism in service of saving the most lives.

segments.title: Listener mail: Brett on albinism
segments.summary: Brett, a listener with albinism, writes in about terminology (albinism versus albino), childhood teasing, light sensitivity, low vision, and how TV portrayals of albino characters, such as hitmen, are unrealistic. Follow-up to an earlier episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail at the show's email address and close the episode.
